subject: how older people are treated at a clinic and what that does to whether they go back
citation: Motsohi T, Namane M, Anele AC, Abbas M, Kalula SZ (2020). Older persons' experience with health care at two primary level clinics in Cape Town, South Africa: a qualitative assessment. BJGP Open 4(3):bjgpopen20X101048. doi:10.3399/bjgpopen20X101048

claims.text: Being examined, listened to, and treated respectfully is the test of care: when staff are too few and complaints are dismissed, patients fall silent or become fed up because they feel unheard
evaluative_rules: Judge care by whether you are examined, listened to, and treated with respect
objections: Will I actually be examined, or just given tablets?
Will they listen to me when I tell them about my body?

readings.text: Someone who says you must just keep your mouth shut because you need the tablets would weigh a new service mainly by whether it still lets them get medication without having to complain or ask for more attention.
If you believe there is no examination and you are just given something, you would look for a new service that makes examination a clear, visible step before any treatment is offered.

Someone who is fed up after asking to be examined and only being examined with clothes on would be cautious about a new service unless it shows that complaints about the body are taken seriously and lead to a different examination.

If you have seen doctors and nurses improvise because there are too few of them, you would weigh a new service by whether it reduces the number of people waiting and still leaves time for a proper examination.

claims.text: Age must not decide whether help is possible: abruptness and refusal toward older patients are read as structural ageism because help is withheld on the basis of age
evaluative_rules: Judge help by whether age is being used to refuse it

readings.text: Someone who has been told to just get out when asking a simple question would weigh any new service by whether it removes the chance of being chased out before being heard.
If a person believes help is withheld because of age, they would look for a new service that does not make age the reason for what is or is not offered.
Someone who sees wheelchair patients not getting first privilege at reception and the doctor would weigh a new service by whether it changes who is seen first.
If an older person has seen a folder put aside after a toilet break, they would weigh a new service by whether it keeps their place when they step away.

claims.text: Fairness is first-come-first-served: a person who arrives after you must be seen after you, because queue order is the measure of right and wrong
evaluative_rules: Judge fairness by queue order, not connections or payments
objections: Will I be seen after someone who came after me?

readings.text: Someone who says what is right is right and what is wrong is wrong would judge any new service by whether it keeps the order of arrival as the only measure of who is seen first.
If a person who comes after me must be seen after me, they would be wary of a new policy that lets staff or others move a later arrival ahead, even when that later arrival has some special reason.
Someone who complains that the one that came afterwards will be seen before the first one would be open to a new service only if it makes the first-come-first-served order visible and enforceable.
If queue order is the measure of right and wrong, they would weigh a new policy by asking whether it removes the power of the person collecting cards to decide who is seen first.

claims.text: Doctor-led examination is the quality benchmark: patients prefer doctors and distrust nurses who dismiss complaints because thorough examination and meaningful attention to complaints define good care
evaluative_rules: Judge provider quality by whether a doctor examines you thoroughly
objections: Will I be seen by a doctor, or dismissed by a nurse?

readings.text: Someone who believes doctors thoroughly examine you would weigh a new service by whether it guarantees a doctor-led examination rather than a nurse-led one.
If you have had a professional nurse dismiss your complaint as nothing that will go away, you would be cautious about a new service that routes first contact through nurses.

Someone who attaches quality to having specific complaints addressed meaningfully would be open to a new service only if it shows how complaints are genuinely acknowledged and treatment adjusted, regardless of who provides it.

If you acknowledge good service from other categories of staff but still hold doctors' qualifications in higher regard, you would weigh a new service by the qualifications of the person assigned to you.

claims.text: Convenience and affordability for elderly people are the access test: distance and transport barriers make a facility unusable because elderly patients cannot reach it
evaluative_rules: Judge access by whether an elderly person can actually get there

readings.text: Someone who sees elderly people walking from the sports ground as unacceptable would weigh a new service by whether it removes the distance and transport barrier for those patients.
If a lift was offered and people did not take that opportunity, a new service would be judged by whether it fits what the community is actually willing to use, not only by its availability.
Someone who notes that elderly patients are also carers for grandchildren would weigh a new service by whether it limits the waiting period at the facility.
If taxis cannot work in another area, a new service would be judged by whether it can be reached without crossing those transport boundaries.

region: Hanover Park and Vanguard community health centres, Cape Town, South Africa
confidence: Four focus groups with 33 patients aged 60 and over (median 66, 76% women) at two public community health centres in low-income Cape Town suburbs, August-November 2017. Mechanisms durable; magnitudes unknown, and both clinics serve one metro, so waiting times and travel details are local.
